evals.name: Design a crash recovery benchmark
evals.prompt: I built a multi-agent coordination system where 12 agents collaborate on code tasks. When an agent crashes, the system redistributes its work using session context. I want to prove this is better than naive reassignment. Design the experiment for me. I can run about 200 trials total.
expected_behaviors: Identifies the assignment unit, estimand, outcome oracle, and dependence before allocating the 200-trial budget; does not assume trials are independent.
Chooses relevant comparison conditions and explains their tuning, resource budget, and limits; a deliberately weak baseline alone cannot support broad superiority.
Separates automated process measures (for example salvage latency) from outcome measures (for example task completion and fidelity) and defines how each is measured.
For human judgments, specifies an anchored rubric, blinding where feasible, rater assignment, disagreement handling, and a scale-appropriate agreement summary without a universal cutoff.
Chooses the analysis and uncertainty method from the design, outcome, pairing/clustering, and prespecified contrasts; explains assumptions rather than routing by latency or normality slogans.
States how primary outcomes and multiplicity will be handled according to the claim family and analysis plan.
Includes threats to validity and limits claims to the tested workload, crash model, and resources.
anti_behaviors: Treats 200 runs as 200 independent units without checking assignment, pairing, or clustering.
Claims general superiority from comparison only with a deliberately weak baseline.
Uses a fixed kappa, run-count, or effect-size threshold as a universal validity gate.
Selects a statistical test solely from a normality test or generic latency rule.
Omits outcome measurement, uncertainty, or relevant threats to validity.

evals.name: Audit suspicious benchmark results
evals.prompt: Here are results from our coordination protocol benchmark: We tested 4 systems across 15 metrics. System D (ours) was statistically significant (p < 0.05) on 6 of 15 metrics. All tests were t-tests. We ran 20 trials per system. Mean latencies: System A 450ms, System B 380ms, System C 520ms, System D 290ms. No confidence intervals or effect sizes reported. What's wrong with this analysis?
expected_behaviors: Asks which hypotheses and contrasts were prespecified and which were chosen after seeing results; separates confirmatory from exploratory claims.
Checks the outcome definitions, experimental unit, assignment, repeated measures, and dependence before interpreting the tests.
Notes that 15 metrics and multiple system contrasts create a multiplicity concern; asks for the declared family and correction or other justified strategy instead of assuming one correction recipe.
Requests raw counts or distributions, effect estimates, and uncertainty appropriate to the design; recognizes that p-values and means alone do not establish practical value.
Examines whether the t-tests match the estimand, assignment, pairing, and outcome distribution; does not route solely via a normality test.
Treats 20 trials per system as insufficient information to declare power or adequacy without the experimental unit, variance, dependence, and target effect/precision.
Keeps any conclusion scoped to the reported systems, metrics, and workload.
anti_behaviors: Accepts significance counts without checking multiplicity and prespecification.
Treats absence of confidence intervals or effects as immaterial.
Rejects t-tests solely because latency is presumed non-normal.
Declares a universal minimum sample size or power conclusion from 20 trials alone.

evals.name: Design human evaluation for salvage fidelity
evals.prompt: We need human raters to judge whether our salvage system recovers agent work faithfully. We have 50 crash-recovery scenarios and outputs from 2 systems. We can recruit 4 raters who are experienced engineers. Design the complete human evaluation protocol, including the rubric, the reliability check, and what to do if raters disagree a lot.
expected_behaviors: Designs an anchored rubric tied to the fidelity construct and preserves examples for each category.
Uses blinded condition labels where feasible and randomizes presentation order or accounts for order effects.
Plans calibration on development examples while keeping any confirmatory evaluation on fresh held-out cases.
Chooses an agreement summary suited to the rating scale, prevalence, missingness, rater assignment, and question; states uncertainty and avoids universal kappa thresholds.
Defines how to record disagreement and when adjudication or consensus is appropriate without treating majority vote as a correctness oracle.
Accounts for rater workload, fatigue, and dependence in assignment and analysis.
Explains how ratings enter the analysis (for example, an aggregation justified by the question or a model representing rater effects).
anti_behaviors: Uses vague categories without behavioral anchors.
Treats one coefficient or cutoff as proof of reliable judgments.
Uses the same examples both to revise the rubric and to make a held-out confirmatory reliability claim.
Hides initial disagreement by reporting only a consensus score.
